claims.text: The Wind Waker project links source-built objects only for units marked complete, uses original extracted objects for the rest, and checks the result against a per-version hash list of 415–417 entries. Its public progress report lists 79.58% of GZLE01 code (32,968 of 39,324 functions) matched, 78.38–78.65% for other retail versions and 74.08% for the demo. Matching is therefore measured and falsifiable per version, not asserted.

claims.text: A shared library can ship under the same identifying name while built in different incompatible modes, and the mismatch only surfaces as crashes or internal errors. So 'same version' is not evidence of 'same behavior' when compiler or build options differ.

claims.text: Microsoft's compiler refuses to link optimized (whole-program/link-time) objects from different toolset versions, down to the minor update: a library built with Visual Studio 2019 16.7 cannot be linked into an app built with 16.8. The fix is rebuilding every object and library with one toolset version. For a studio copying a library between game projects, a compiler patch bump therefore forces a rebuild rather than a quiet mismatch, at least for these optimization modes.

meta.capability: You can expect toolchain-version mismatches in optimized builds to be caught loudly at build time, and budget a full rebuild of reused libraries after any compiler update instead of hunting for silent faults.

claims.text: When two versions or flavors of one library end up in the same program, the system often does not complain; which one wins depends on load order, and differences in internal data layout can silently corrupt memory. Even a tool as common as gdb pulled in 18 direct libraries and 265 entries counting duplicates, so accidental mixes are easy. Distributions avoid this by shipping one version of each library, and even the Nix package system is not immune if overrides are applied inconsistently.

claims.text: Fuzzy function matching compares code by similarity and confidence rather than exact bytes, so it tolerates unknown compiler options, instruction-set differences and light patches. In the ESP32 example, matches against a reference build still succeed with other releases in the same major series, just with lower confidence, which makes the approach useful when the firmware has no clear version indicators. The older exact-match approach needs a new database for every change in target or compiler flags, which is rarely knowable from a firmware dump.

claims.text: Small getters, setters and constant-returning routines score high on similarity but low on confidence, so they are poor evidence of which library or version is present. Progress reporting should therefore require a full-image comparison, not a per-function similarity score.

Of 320 failed builds, 34% were blueprint gaps, versus 38% AI mistakes. Of attempts, only about 3 in 100 succeed, so removing systemic blockers pays more than retrying.

meta.capability: You can direct effort toward fixing shared foundations, such as class declarations, instead of grinding on individual failing functions, because one fix unblocks many.

claims.text: The shared approach starts costing more than it saves when teams become afraid to touch the library for fear of breaking other applications. That fear produces workarounds and informal shadow copies with slight variations, so the split happens de facto before anyone decides it. Making the split deliberate at that point is cheaper than letting uncontrolled forks accumulate.

meta.query: Why do projects that began with one shared library repository for several games end up splitting it into separate per-game copies, and at what point in the work did the shared approach start costing more than it saved?
meta.capability: You can treat a shared library's 'safe-to-change' status as a leading indicator, and approve a split into per-product copies once teams start fearing edits, rather than waiting for a visible outage.

claims.text: Applications rarely have identical needs, so a shared library grows into a bloated catch-all trying to serve everyone. Its pace is also set by the slowest, most complex consumer, which slows delivery for simpler, faster-moving teams. For a studio with several games, the cost of sharing falls hardest on the game with the most divergent or fastest-moving requirements.

meta.capability: You can stop assuming that separate projects want the same shared code, and require a few games to prove identical needs before funding a common library.

claims.text: The contents describe a spectrum of structures: submodules for fully independent projects, subtrees for one repo with external sources, and a monorepo for tightly related projects that benefit from shared tooling. They also note that monorepos grow very large and need discipline and tooling. None says when a game studio should leave a shared structure, so the trigger point remains unconfirmed by this research.
